Option B collapses all four distinct checks into one, ignoring that they operate at completely different pipeline stages (before retrieval, during document filtering, after generation for factual accuracy, and after generation for user-need satisfaction). Option C incorrectly merges Grounding and Usefulness, when the notes explicitly distinguish them with the phrase 'grounded ≠ useful' specifically to prevent this exact conflation — an answer can pass IsSUP but still fail IsUSE. Option D swaps the definitions of Routing and Grounding entirely, backwards from their documented, explicit descriptions.

question: Self-RAG's decision flow has bounded retry loops: revise_answer loops up to max 10 retries (triggered by is_sup), and rewrite_question loops up to max 3 retries (triggered by is_use). Why are these loops explicitly BOUNDED rather than allowed to retry indefinitely?
options: A) Bounding the retries prevents infinite loops — if an answer can't be made grounded/useful within the retry limit, the flow falls through to no_answer_found rather than looping forever chasing an unattainable perfect answer
B) The retry limits exist purely as a UI display feature, with no actual effect on execution flow
C) Unbounded retries would be strictly better; the max 10 / max 3 limits are described as bugs in the current implementation
D) revise_answer and rewrite_question loops never actually terminate; the max retry counts are purely aspirational documentation with no enforcement
explanation: The notes explicitly justify the bounding: for is_sup, '↻ loop, max 10 retries' on revise_answer, and the key gates explanation states 'is_sup (grounding) → ... triggers revise_answer loop (bounded: max 10 retries) if not fully grounded'; similarly for is_use, 'rewrite_question (bounded: max 3 rewrite tries) → prevents infinite loop, falls to no_answer_found if exhausted.' The explicit design intent is preventing infinite loops — since both grounding and usefulness are judged by the LLM itself (which may never converge to a 'perfect' answer for a genuinely hard or unanswerable query), an unbounded retry loop could spin forever chasing an unattainable standard, burning compute/API calls with no termination guarantee. Bounding the retries with a clear fallback (no_answer_found once exhausted) ensures the system ALWAYS terminates with some defined outcome, even if that outcome is an honest 'I don't have a good answer' rather than an endless retry spiral. Option B dismisses this as cosmetic, contradicting the explicit, functional 'prevents infinite loop' rationale and the fallback state (no_answer_found) that only makes sense as an actual enforced execution-flow behavior. Option C incorrectly frames bounding as a bug rather than the deliberate safety mechanism it's documented as being — unbounded retries would actually be WORSE from a reliability and cost-control standpoint, not better. Option D denies enforcement entirely, contradicting the explicit graph structure showing these as real, bounded loops with defined exit conditions (reaching the retry cap routes to no_answer_found), not merely aspirational text.

question: What is the key architectural difference between CRAG and Self-RAG, per the notes' explicit comparison?
options: A) CRAG corrects RETRIEVAL quality (via web search fallback when internal docs fail evaluation); Self-RAG adds self-verification of the LLM's OWN GENERATION (groundedness + usefulness), with bounded retry loops at multiple stages — not just correcting retrieval
B) CRAG and Self-RAG are functionally identical architectures with only naming differences
C) Self-RAG only corrects retrieval quality; CRAG is the one that verifies the LLM's own generated answer
D) Neither architecture involves any kind of LLM self-judgment; both rely purely on fixed, rule-based thresholds with no reflective questioning at all
explanation: The notes state the key difference explicitly: 'KEY DIFF vs CRAG → CRAG corrects retrieval quality (web search fallback); Self-RAG adds self-verification of the LLM's OWN generation (groundedness + usefulness), with bounded retry loops at multiple stages, not just retrieval.' CRAG's fixes are concentrated on the RETRIEVAL side of the pipeline — evaluating whether retrieved docs are good enough, and if not, correcting course via query rewriting and web search fallback — but CRAG's flow, once it reaches generate, doesn't explicitly loop back to re-examine or revise the GENERATED answer itself. Self-RAG goes further, adding explicit self-reflection AFTER generation too — checking groundedness (IsSUP) and usefulness (IsUSE) of the actual produced answer, with bounded retry mechanisms (revise_answer, rewrite_question) that can loop the process multiple times specifically to improve the GENERATION quality itself, not just the retrieval inputs feeding into it. Option B denies a real, explicitly documented architectural distinction the notes draw specifically to differentiate the two approaches. Option C exactly swaps the two architectures' actual specializations, backwards from the documented comparison. Option D is false for both architectures; CRAG explicitly uses an LLM-based (or T5-based) Retrieval Evaluator to SCORE document relevance (a form of LLM judgment, even if threshold-gated), and Self-RAG's entire premise is built around LLM self-reflection questions (Routing, Relevance, Grounding, Usefulness) — both architectures fundamentally rely on some form of LLM-driven judgment, not purely fixed rules with zero reflective component.
